unit.name: Ecological Adaptations, Succession and Ecological Services (Botany)

chapter: Ecological Adaptations, Succession and Ecological Services
question_text: What are hydrophytes? Briefly discuss the different kinds of hydrophytes with examples.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack botany section, Chapter 13, book p.36, SAQ 2. All five of the book's kinds and its examples are kept (Pistia and Lemna; Nelumbo; Hydrilla; Vallisneria; Limnophila), with one extra standard example added to each line. Only one source book is held for botany — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand is physics-only and no botany board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card, not merely unrun. The 1+1+1+1 split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

page_header: Ecological Adaptations, Succession and Ecological Services · 4 marks

steps.label: Definition and the five kinds
lines: Hydrophytes are plants that grow in water
steps.why: The two questions asked here are the definition and the list, so both belong in the opening block. The five kinds are separated by only two facts: whether the plant is rooted, and whether it floats or is submerged.
common_mistakes: Giving four kinds. The standard count in this syllabus is five.
Defining hydrophytes as water plants only. Very wet soil counts too, which is why amphibious plants belong here.
steps.memory_tip: Two questions sort all five: rooted or not, floating or submerged. The fifth is the in-between one, amphibious.
steps.margin_note: Definition in one line, then the numbered list. This block is one mark.

steps.label: The two floating kinds
lines: Free floating hydrophytes: float freely on
the water surface with no contact with the
rooted in the mud, with long petioles that
hold the leaves on the surface.
steps.why: Both kinds have leaves on the surface; the difference is the root. Free floating plants touch no soil, while the second kind is fixed in the mud and reaches the surface by a long petiole.
common_mistakes: Putting Nelumbo in the free floating group. Nelumbo is rooted in the mud.
Leaving out the words no contact with soil, which is the whole definition of free floating.
steps.memory_tip: Both float; only one is tied down. Pistia drifts, Nelumbo is anchored.
steps.margin_note: One line of definition and one example line per kind.

steps.label: The two submerged kinds
lines: under water with no contact with soil.
water and fixed to the soil by roots.
steps.why: The same root test separates these two as separated the floating pair, so the four kinds form a neat two by two table: floating or submerged, rooted or not.
common_mistakes: Writing that submerged plants have stomata. Submerged leaves have no stomata.
Swapping Hydrilla and Vallisneria. Hydrilla is suspended, Vallisneria is rooted.
steps.memory_tip: Hydrilla hangs, Vallisneria is fixed. Both stay under water.
steps.margin_note: Keep the wording parallel with the floating block; parallel lines read as four clear kinds.

steps.label: Amphibious plants

lines.text: Amphibious: partly in water, partly in air

lines: The lower part of the plant stands in water
or wet mud and the upper part is in the
air, so it bears two kinds of leaves.
steps.why: Amphibious plants are the fifth kind because they belong to neither water nor land alone, and their two leaf forms on one plant are the visible proof of it.
common_mistakes: Leaving this kind out. It is the one most often forgotten of the five.
Calling them mesophytes. A mesophyte grows in ordinary moist soil, not standing water.
steps.memory_tip: Amphibious means living in both water and air — the same word is used for frogs.
steps.margin_note: Two lines and one example finish the answer; do not extend past four blocks.

insider_note: The list is what carries the marks here, not the description. Write all five names first, then one line and one example each — a long account of two kinds and silence on the rest scores less.
